1.  **Chance creation at the Women's Euro, randomization test.** The book's flagship regression — goals on accumulated chance quality — was tested at the 2022 Men's World Cup in @sec-randslope.
    Per this book's replication habit, we now ask whether the relationship holds at the 2025 Women's Euro.
    The code below aggregates the tournament's 913 shots into 62 team-matches (unlike the World Cup's 127, no side finished a Euro match without a shot); per the penalty convention, note the frame: the shot log counts in-game penalties and shoot-out kicks in both `total_xg` and `goals`, on both sides of the model.[^_24-ex-inf-model-slr-7]
    Shown below are the linear model output for predicting goals from total xG and a summary of the slopes from 1,000 randomized datasets (1,000 times, `goals` was permuted and regressed against `total_xg`).[^_24-ex-inf-model-slr-1]

    ```r
    weuro2025_shots <- read_csv("data/derived/weuro2025_shots.csv")

    team_match_weuro <- weuro2025_shots |>
      group_by(match_id, team) |>
      summarize(
        n_shots = n(),
        total_xg = sum(statsbomb_xg),
        goals = sum(goal),
        .groups = "drop"
      )

    fit_weuro_xg <- lm(goals ~ total_xg, data = team_match_weuro)
    tidy(fit_weuro_xg)
    #> # A tibble: 2 × 5
    #>   term        estimate std.error statistic  p.value
    #>   <chr>          <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>
    #> 1 (Intercept)    0.423    0.208       2.03 4.63e- 2
    #> 2 total_xg       0.785    0.0777     10.1  1.43e-14

    set.seed(2410)
    weuro_slope_null <- team_match_weuro |>
      specify(goals ~ total_xg) |>
      hypothesize(null = "independence") |>
      generate(reps = 1000, type = "permute") |>
      calculate(stat = "slope")
    ```

    A histogram of the 1,000 randomized slopes is centered at 0 and ranges from $-0.34$ to $+0.40$; a red vertical line drawn at the observed slope of $0.785$ sits far outside the histogram, and none of the 1,000 randomized slopes was at least as far from zero.

    a.  What are the null and alternative hypotheses for evaluating whether the slope of the model predicting a team's goals from its accumulated chance quality is different than 0?

    b.  Using the histogram which describes the distribution of slopes when the null hypothesis is true, find the p-value and conclude the hypothesis test in the context of the problem (use words like chance quality and goals).

    c.  Is the conclusion based on the histogram of randomized slopes consistent with the conclusion the mathematical model would have reached?
        Explain your reasoning.

2.  **Fatigue drift at the Women's Euro, randomization test.** In @sec-bootbeta1 the fatigue-drift theory — chances get better as the match wears on — collapsed on the World Cup's open-play shots.
    Here we study the same relationship at the 2025 Women's Euro, on the same frame as @sec-bootbeta1, per the book's penalty convention: `shot_type == "Open Play"` (851 shots), stated because penalty kicks carry a fixed chance quality and the shoot-out kicks sit at the very end of the clock.
    Shown below are the linear model output for predicting chance quality (xG) from the minute of the match and a summary of the slopes from 1,000 randomized datasets (1,000 times, `statsbomb_xg` was permuted and regressed against `minute`).[^_24-ex-inf-model-slr-2]

    ```r
    weuro_open <- weuro2025_shots |>
      filter(shot_type == "Open Play")

    fit_weuro_minute <- lm(statsbomb_xg ~ minute, data = weuro_open)
    tidy(fit_weuro_minute)
    #> # A tibble: 2 × 5
    #>   term         estimate std.error statistic  p.value
    #>   <chr>           <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>
    #> 1 (Intercept)  0.104     0.00791     13.1   4.88e-36
    #> 2 minute      -0.000125  0.000132    -0.951 3.42e- 1

    set.seed(2411)
    weuro_minute_null <- weuro_open |>
      specify(statsbomb_xg ~ minute) |>
      hypothesize(null = "independence") |>
      generate(reps = 1000, type = "permute") |>
      calculate(stat = "slope")
    ```

    A histogram of the 1,000 randomized slopes is centered at 0 and ranges from $-0.00042$ to $+0.00039$; a red vertical line drawn at the observed slope of $-0.000125$ falls well inside the histogram, and 363 of the 1,000 randomized slopes were at least as far from zero as the observed slope.

    a.  What are the null and alternative hypotheses for evaluating whether the slope of the model predicting a shot's chance quality from the minute of the match is different than 0?
        Note that at this tournament the observed drift runs *downhill* — the opposite sign to the World Cup's.

    b.  Using the randomized slopes, find the p-value and conclude the hypothesis test in the context of the problem (use words like minute and chance quality).
        What does the conclusion of your test say about whether the match clock is a useful predictor of chance quality?

    c.  Is the conclusion based on the histogram of randomized slopes consistent with the conclusion from the mathematical model?
        Explain your reasoning.

3.  **Shot volume and chance quality at the Women's Euro, mathematical test.** Does a team's shot count in a match predict how much chance quality it accumulates?
    The scatterplot and least squares summary below show the relationship between the number of shots and the total xG across the 62 team-matches of the 2025 Women's Euro (all-shots frame, as in Exercise 1).[^_24-ex-inf-model-slr-7]
    The 62 points climb from quiet outings of 4 shots and under 0.5 xG toward high-volume performances of up to 34 shots, with total xG reaching 7.4; the cloud spreads noticeably as the shot counts grow.

    ```r
    fit_weuro_shots <- lm(total_xg ~ n_shots, data = team_match_weuro)
    tidy(fit_weuro_shots)
    #> # A tibble: 2 × 5
    #>   term        estimate std.error statistic      p.value
    #>   <chr>          <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>        <dbl>
    #> 1 (Intercept)   -0.491    0.436      -1.13 0.265
    #> 2 n_shots        0.168    0.0270      6.24 0.0000000481
    ```

    a.  Describe the relationship between the number of shots and total chance quality.

    b.  Write the equation of the regression line.
        Interpret the slope and intercept in context.

    c.  Do the data provide convincing evidence that the true slope parameter is different than 0?
        State the null and alternative hypotheses, report the p-value (using a mathematical model), and state your conclusion.

    d.  The correlation coefficient between the number of shots and total xG is 0.63.
        Calculate $R^2$ and interpret it in context.

5.  **Chance creation at the Women's Euro, bootstrap percentile interval.** In order to estimate the slope of the model predicting a team's goals from its accumulated chance quality, 1,000 bootstrap samples are taken from the 62 team-matches of the 2025 Women's Euro.
    A linear model predicting `goals` from `total_xg` is fit to each bootstrap sample, and the slope is estimated.

    ```r
    set.seed(2412)
    weuro_slope_boot <- team_match_weuro |>
      specify(goals ~ total_xg) |>
      generate(reps = 1000, type = "bootstrap") |>
      calculate(stat = "slope")
    ```

    The histogram of the 1,000 bootstrapped slopes is bell-shaped, running from 0.55 to 1.32; its 1st and 99th percentiles are 0.598 and 1.087.

    a.  Using the bootstrap percentile method, find a 98% confidence interval for the slope parameter.

    b.  Interpret the confidence interval in the context of the problem.

11. **Twenty matches, randomization test.** Priya Rao pulls a random sample of 20 matches from the 2022 Men's World Cup and asks the chapter's headline question at the level of whole matches: does the combined chance quality of a match predict its combined goal count?
    Both totals are computed from the shot log for regulation and extra time (shoot-out kicks excluded, so both sides of the model live on the same frame; in-game penalties included in both).
    Shown below are the linear model output and a summary of the slopes from 1,000 randomized datasets (1,000 times, `match_goals` was permuted and regressed against `match_xg`).[^_24-ex-inf-model-slr-3]

    ```r
    wc2022_shots <- read_csv("data/derived/wc2022_shots.csv")

    wc_match_xg <- wc2022_shots |>
      filter(period <= 4) |>
      group_by(match_id) |>
      summarize(
        match_goals = sum(goal),
        match_xg = sum(statsbomb_xg),
        .groups = "drop"
      )

    set.seed(2414)
    matches20 <- wc_match_xg |> slice_sample(n = 20)

    fit_matches20 <- lm(match_goals ~ match_xg, data = matches20)
    tidy(fit_matches20)
    #> # A tibble: 2 × 5
    #>   term        estimate std.error statistic p.value
    #>   <chr>          <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>
    #> 1 (Intercept)    0.238     0.966     0.247 0.808
    #> 2 match_xg       1.10      0.330     3.35  0.00356

    set.seed(2415)
    matches20_null <- matches20 |>
      specify(match_goals ~ match_xg) |>
      hypothesize(null = "independence") |>
      generate(reps = 1000, type = "permute") |>
      calculate(stat = "slope")
    ```

    A histogram of the 1,000 randomized slopes is centered at 0 and ranges from $-1.22$ to $+1.24$; a red vertical line drawn at the observed slope of $1.10$ sits in its extreme right tail, and 5 of the 1,000 randomized slopes were at least as far from zero.

    a.  What are the null and alternative hypotheses for evaluating whether the slope of the model predicting a match's combined goals from its combined chance quality is different than 0?

    b.  Using the histogram which describes the distribution of slopes when the null hypothesis is true, find the p-value and conclude the hypothesis test in the context of the problem.

    c.  Is the conclusion based on the histogram of randomized slopes consistent with the conclusion which would have been obtained using the mathematical model?
        Explain your reasoning.

16. **Shot volume and chance quality, World Cup.** Across the 127 team-matches of the 2022 Men's World Cup (the canonical `team_match` data, all-shots frame), a linear model is built to predict a team's accumulated chance quality (`total_xg`) from its number of shots (`n_shots`).
    The table below shows the model output.[^_24-ex-inf-model-slr-4]

    ```r
    team_match <- wc2022_shots |>
      group_by(match_id, team) |>
      summarize(
        n_shots = n(),
        total_xg = sum(statsbomb_xg),
        goals = sum(goal),
        prop_under_pressure = mean(under_pressure),
        prop_set_piece = mean(play_pattern %in%
          c("From Corner", "From Free Kick", "From Throw In")),
        .groups = "drop"
      )

    fit_wc_shots <- lm(total_xg ~ n_shots, data = team_match)
    tidy(fit_wc_shots)
    #> # A tibble: 2 × 5
    #>   term        estimate std.error statistic  p.value
    #>   <chr>          <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>
    #> 1 (Intercept)   -0.326    0.182      -1.79 7.65e- 2
    #> 2 n_shots        0.154    0.0140     10.9  6.01e-20
    ```

    a.  What are the hypotheses for evaluating whether shot volume is positively associated with accumulated chance quality?

    b.  State the conclusion of the hypothesis test from part (a) in context.

    c.  Calculate a 95% confidence interval for the slope of `n_shots`, and interpret it in context.
        (The model's degrees of freedom are $127 - 2 = 125,$ and $t^{\star}_{125} = 1.98.$)

    d.  Do your results from the hypothesis test and the confidence interval agree?
        Explain your reasoning.

17. **Extra finishing sessions.** Jonas Beck suspects that the number of extra finishing sessions an academy forward completes each month drives the improvement in the club's standardized finishing assessment (scored in points).
    To find out, sixteen academy forwards were *randomly assigned* a number of extra sessions for one month — between 1 and 9 — on top of the common program, and their assessment gains were recorded.
    This is a constructed Northbridge scenario, built by the seeded code below; the scatterplot shows the sixteen points climbing steadily with the session count, and the regression table summarizes the fit.[^_24-ex-inf-model-slr-5]

    ```r
    set.seed(2417)
    drill16 <- tibble(
      sessions = sample(1:9, 16, replace = TRUE),
      gain     = round(1 + 2.2 * sessions + rnorm(16, mean = 0, sd = 3), 1)
    )

    fit_drill <- lm(gain ~ sessions, data = drill16)
    tidy(fit_drill)
    #> # A tibble: 2 × 5
    #>   term        estimate std.error statistic    p.value
    #>   <chr>          <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>      <dbl>
    #> 1 (Intercept)     1.79     1.60       1.12 0.282
    #> 2 sessions        2.19     0.279      7.85 0.00000170
    ```

    a.  Describe the relationship between the number of extra sessions and the assessment gain.

    b.  Write the equation of the regression line.
        Interpret the slope and intercept in context.

    c.  Do the data provide convincing evidence that completing more extra sessions is associated with a larger assessment gain?
        State the null and alternative hypotheses, report the p-value, and state your conclusion.
        Given the design of the study, can the conclusion be causal?

    d.  The correlation coefficient for sessions and gain is 0.90.
        Calculate $R^2$ and interpret it in context.

    e.  Suppose Priya instead scraped a league-wide database of academy forwards who *choose* their own number of extra sessions, and regressed their assessment gains on their session counts.
        Would the relationship between sessions and gains be as strong as the relationship found in Jonas's study?
        Why?

[^_24-ex-inf-model-slr-1]: The 2025 Women's Euro shot data used in this exercise are in `data/derived/weuro2025_shots.csv` (StatsBomb open data); `team_match_weuro` aggregates them by match and team.

[^_24-ex-inf-model-slr-2]: The 2025 Women's Euro shot data used in this exercise are in `data/derived/weuro2025_shots.csv` (StatsBomb open data).

[^_24-ex-inf-model-slr-3]: The 2022 Men's World Cup shot data used in this exercise are in `data/derived/wc2022_shots.csv` (StatsBomb open data).

[^_24-ex-inf-model-slr-4]: The `team_match` data are the book's canonical aggregate of `data/derived/wc2022_shots.csv` (StatsBomb open data), rebuilt with the code shown in @sec-randslope; the all-shots frame (penalties and shoot-out kicks included on both sides of the model) travels with the object.

[^_24-ex-inf-model-slr-5]: The `drill16` data are a constructed scouting scenario, generated entirely by the seeded code shown; no real academy players were assessed.

[^_24-ex-inf-model-slr-6]: The team shot profiles are computed from `data/derived/wc2022_shots.csv` (StatsBomb open data) with the `team_profile` code of @sec-data-hello and @sec-fit-line-res-cor.

[^_24-ex-inf-model-slr-7]: A caution that travels with every `team_match`-style aggregate, per the Data callout of @sec-randslope: the `goals` column sums the shot log's goal flags, so it counts converted shoot-out kicks too — it is not the recorded match score.
